title: Moons of Jupiter
description: Natural satellites of the planet Jupiter
wiki_lead:
There are 115 known moons of the planet Jupiter as of 9 April 2026. This number does not include a number of meter-sized moonlets thought to be shed from the inner moons, nor hundreds of possible kilometer-sized outer irregular moons that were only briefly captured by telescopes. All together, Jupiter's moons form a satellite system, colloquially referred to as the Jovian system. The most massive of the moons are the four Galilean moons: Io, Europa, Ganymede, and Callisto, all of which were independently discovered in 1610 by Galileo Galilei and Simon Marius and were the first objects found to orbit a body that was neither Earth nor the Sun. Much more recently, beginning in 1892, dozens of far smaller Jovian moons have been detected and have received the names of lovers (or other sexual partners) or daughters of the Roman god Jupiter or his Greek equivalent Zeus. The Galilean moons are by far the largest and most massive objects to orbit Jupiter, with the remaining 111 known moons and the rings together comprising just 0.003% of the total orbiting mass.
Of Jupiter's moons, eight are regular satellites with prograde and nearly circular orbits that are not greatly inclined with respect to Jupiter's equatorial plane. The Galilean satellites are nearly spherical in shape due to their planetary mass, and are just massive enough that they would be considered planets if they were in direct orbit around the Sun. The other four regular satellites, known as the inner moons, are much smaller and closer to Jupiter; these serve as sources of the dust that makes up Jupiter's rings. The remainder of Jupiter's moons are outer irregular satellites whose prograde and retrograde orbits are much farther from Jupiter and have high inclinations and eccentricities. The largest of these moons were likely asteroids that were captured from solar orbits by Jupiter before impacts with other small bodies shattered them into many kilometer-sized fragments, forming collisional families of moons sharing similar orbits. Jupiter is expected to have about 100 irregular moons larger than 1 km (0.6 mi) in diameter, plus around 500 more smaller retrograde moons down to diameters of 0.8 km (0.5 mi). Of the 107 known irregular moons of Jupiter, 58 of them have not yet been officially given names.

Characteristics

The physical and orbital characteristics of the moons vary widely. The four Galileans are all over 3,100 kilometres (1,900 mi) in diameter; the largest Galilean, Ganymede, is the ninth largest object in the Solar System, after the Sun and seven of the planets, Ganymede being larger than Mercury. All other Jovian moons are less than 250 kilometres (160 mi) in diameter, with most barely exceeding 5 kilometres (3.1 mi). Their orbital shapes range from nearly perfectly circular to highly eccentric and inclined, and many revolve in the direction opposite to Jupiter's rotation (retrograde motion).

grok_lead: The moons of Jupiter are the natural satellites orbiting the gas giant Jupiter, comprising a diverse system of 101 bodies officially recognized by the International Astronomical Union as of March 2026. This includes four newly confirmed irregular moons announced by the Minor Planet Center on March 16, 2026, surpassing the previous count of 95 (as of 2025) and marking the first time Jupiter's known moons exceed 100. These include four large, geologically active Galilean moons âIo, Europa, Ganymede, and Callistoâdiscovered in 1610 by Galileo Galilei, which together account for much of the system's mass and scientific interest due to their varied surfaces, subsurface oceans, and potential for habitability. The remaining moons are smaller and mostly irregular in shape, forming part of a complex orbital architecture that reveals Jupiter's gravitational influence and history of capturing asteroids. Jupiter's moons are broadly classified into inner moons, the Galilean satellites, outer regular moons, and irregular moons, reflecting their orbital proximity, size, and dynamical origins. The four inner moonsâMetis, Adrastea, Amalthea, and Thebeâorbit close to Jupiter within its ring system, are irregularly shaped, and range from about 16 to 167 kilometers in diameter; they were discovered between 1892 and 1979 using ground-based and Voyager spacecraft observations. The Galilean moons, orbiting farther out at distances of about 422,000 to 1,883,000 kilometers, are spherical due to their size (diameters ranging from 3,122 km for Europa to 5,268 km for Ganymede, the largest moon in the solar system, with Callisto at 4,821 km) and exhibit remarkable diversity: Io is the most volcanically active body known, Europa likely harbors a global ocean beneath its icy crust, Ganymede has its own magnetic field, and Callisto features ancient, cratered terrain. Beyond these, Jupiter has a handful of outer regular moons in prograde orbits, such as Himalia and Elara (discovered in 1904â1905), which are part of larger groupings like the Himalia group, but the majorityâover 80âare distant irregular moons with highly inclined and often retrograde orbits, suggesting they were captured from the asteroid belt or resulted from collisions. These smaller satellites, many under 10 kilometers across and provisionally designated (e.g., S/2022 J1), were mostly identified in the 20th and 21st centuries through deep imaging surveys, highlighting Jupiter's role in shaping the outer solar system's debris. Missions like NASA's Galileo (1995â2003), Juno (ongoing since 2016), and the Europa Clipper (launched 2024) have provided detailed insights into the moons' compositions, atmospheres, and interactions with Jupiter's magnetosphere, underscoring their importance for understanding planetary formation and astrobiology.
